subtype: Approach: role-play practice of saying no loudly [Action]
passage: Sit down, children; I, Eshaan Sir, want to tell you about the safety practice we used to do at my school. Every Friday we made a game of it. One child played the stranger, and the others shouted "NO!" as loud as their chests would allow, then ran to me at the blackboard. Some of them giggled. Ritu, ten years old, giggled the most. Months later, at the fair, a man took hold of her sleeve and told her to come along. Ritu did not freeze. She shouted "NO!" so the whole lane turned, and ran to a shopkeeper. The practice had done the thinking for her legs.

qa.q: What did the children do in the Friday practice?
qa.a: One child played the stranger and the others shouted "NO!" as loud as they could, then ran to the teacher.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been feeling when the man took hold of her sleeve?
qa.a: Frightened, most likely, but the practice kept her from freezing.

qa.q: What choice did Ritu make at the fair, and why did it help?
qa.a: She shouted "NO!" so the whole lane turned and ran to a shopkeeper, and having practised made it a habit she could use.

qa.q: How does Eshaan Sir see the giggling during the practice?
qa.a: He seems to accept it as part of the game, since practice can be light and still work when it counts.

grounding: Children practise shouting no and running to a teacher, so a real situation brings a rehearsed response.

subtype: Approach: role-play practice of saying no loudly [Action]
passage: The school hall was so noisy with rain on the roof that Maria Miss had to use a whistle. "Today we practise saying no. Loud enough to beat the rain." She stood in for a stranger. "Come with me, I've got a puppy." Pallavi, who spoke so quietly that teachers leaned in to hear her, was first. She opened her mouth. "No," she whispered. "Again. Like you mean it." "No!" "From your belly!" "NO!" Pallavi's own voice startled her. "Now run to me." Maria Miss stepped back to the corner, and Pallavi ran to her. By the end of the lesson every child had done it three times, even the quiet ones, and the hall rang with no.

qa.q: What did Maria Miss say she had, when playing the stranger?
qa.a: She said she had a puppy.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when her own voice startled her?
qa.a: She was surprised and a little proud, finding she could be loud when she needed to be.

qa.q: What else could the class practise, and why?
qa.a: They could practise telling a trusted adult afterwards, because saying no and running is only the first step.

qa.q: How does the practice look to Maria Miss?
qa.a: Maria Miss is pleased to see even the quiet children find their loud voices, which is the point of rehearsing.

grounding: It shows children practising a firm, loud no and running to the teacher so the response becomes a rehearsed habit.

subtype: Approach: role-play practice of saying no loudly [Action]
passage: In the Class 4 room of a Hyderabad school, Jomon sir pushed back the desks. "If someone you don't know says 'come with me', what do you do?" "Say no?" said Rafiq. "Show me. Loud." "No!" "Louder. Then run to a teacher." Rafiq shouted, "NO!" and ran to the back of the room where Jomon sir stood. The class clapped. They did it again and again, in pairs, until it felt ordinary. "Why practise so much?" Rafiq asked. "Because when you're scared, you freeze," Jomon sir said. "If you've done it fifty times, your body remembers." At the end of the lesson, Rafiq said his no so loudly that the teacher next door poked her head in.

qa.q: Where did Rafiq run to after shouting no?
qa.a: To the back of the room where Jomon sir stood.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq ask why they practised so much?
qa.a: He was curious and maybe a bit bored by the repeating, wanting to understand the reason.

qa.q: What else could the class practise, and why?
qa.a: They could practise telling a parent or teacher what happened afterwards, because telling is part of staying safe.

qa.q: How does the practice look to the teacher next door?
qa.a: The teacher next door is startled by the loud no and curious, so it shows how strong the habit is getting.

grounding: It shows children practising a loud, firm no and running to a teacher so the response becomes a rehearsed habit.
